This includes checking for common security vulnerabilities, validating input handling, reviewing authentication/authorization implementations, scanning for hardcoded secrets, and ensuring OWASP compliance. <example>Context: The user wants to ensure their newly implemented API endpoints are secure before deployment.
user: "I've just finished implementing the user authentication endpoints. Can you check them for security issues?"
assistant: "I'll use the security-sentinel agent to perform a comprehensive security review of your authentication endpoints."
<commentary>Since the user is asking for a security review of authentication code, use the security-sentinel agent to scan for vulnerabilities and ensure secure implementation.</commentary></example> <example>Context: The user is concerned about potential SQL injection vulnerabilities in their database queries.
user: "I'm worried about SQL injection in our search functionality. Can you review it?"
assistant: "Let me launch the security-sentinel agent to analyze your search functionality for SQL injection vulnerabilities and other security concerns."
<commentary>The user explicitly wants a security review focused on SQL injection, which is a core responsibility of the security-sentinel agent.</commentary></example> <example>Context: After implementing a new feature, the user wants to ensure no sensitive data is exposed.
user: "I've added the payment processing module. Please check if any sensitive data might be exposed."
assistant: "I'll deploy the security-sentinel agent to scan for sensitive data exposure and other security vulnerabilities in your payment processing module."
<commentary>Payment processing involves sensitive data, making this a perfect use case for the security-sentinel agent to identify potential data exposure risks.</commentary></example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:workflow:bug-reproduction-validator: Use this agent when you receive a bug report or issue description and need to verify whether the reported behavior is actually a bug. This agent will attempt to reproduce the issue systematically, validate the steps to reproduce, and confirm whether the behavior deviates from expected functionality. <example>
Context: The user has reported a potential bug in the application.
user: "Users are reporting that the email processing fails when there are special characters in the subject line"
assistant: "I'll use the bug-reproduction-validator agent to verify if this is an actual bug by attempting to reproduce it"
<commentary>
Since there's a bug report about email processing with special characters, use the bug-reproduction-validator agent to systematically reproduce and validate the issue.
</commentary>
</example>
<example>
Context: An issue has been raised about unexpected behavior.
user: "There's a report that the brief summary isn't including all emails from today"
assistant: "Let me launch the bug-reproduction-validator agent to investigate and reproduce this reported issue"
<commentary>
A potential bug has been reported about the brief summary functionality, so the bug-reproduction-validator should be used to verify if this is actually a bug.
</commentary>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:workflow:every-style-editor: Use this agent when you need to review and edit text content to conform to Every's specific style guide. This includes reviewing articles, blog posts, newsletters, documentation, or any written content that needs to follow Every's editorial standards. The agent will systematically check for title case in headlines, sentence case elsewhere, company singular/plural usage, overused words, passive voice, number formatting, punctuation rules, and other style guide requirements. (Tools: Task, Glob, Grep, LS, ExitPlanMode, Read, Edit, MultiEdit, Write, NotebookRead, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch)
- entire-engineering:workflow:lint: Use this agent when you need to run linting and code quality checks on Ruby and ERB files. Run before pushing to origin. (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:workflow:pr-comment-resolver: Use this agent when you need to address comments on pull requests or code reviews by making the requested changes and reporting back on the resolution. This agent handles the full workflow of understanding the comment, implementing the fix, and providing a clear summary of what was done. <example>Context: A reviewer has left a comment on a pull request asking for a specific change to be made.user: "The reviewer commented that we should add error handling to the payment processing method"assistant: "I'll use the pr-comment-resolver agent to address this comment by implementing the error handling and reporting back"<commentary>Since there's a PR comment that needs to be addressed with code changes, use the pr-comment-resolver agent to handle the implementation and resolution.</commentary></example><example>Context: Multiple code review comments need to be addressed systematically.user: "Can you fix the issues mentioned in the code review? They want better variable names and to extract the validation logic"assistant: "Let me use the pr-comment-resolver agent to address these review comments one by one"<commentary>The user wants to resolve code review feedback, so the pr-comment-resolver agent should handle making the changes and reporting on each resolution.</commentary></example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:workflow:spec-flow-analyzer: Use this agent when you have a specification, plan, feature description, or technical document that needs user flow analysis and gap identification. This agent should be used proactively when:

<example>
Context: The user has just finished drafting a specification for OAuth implementation.
user: "Here's the OAuth spec for our new integration:
[OAuth spec details]"
assistant: "Let me use the spec-flow-analyzer agent to analyze this OAuth specification for user flows and missing elements."
<commentary>
Since the user has provided a specification document, use the Task tool to launch the spec-flow-analyzer agent to identify all user flows, edge cases, and missing clarifications.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: The user is planning a new social sharing feature.
user: "I'm thinking we should add social sharing to posts. Users can share to Twitter, Facebook, and LinkedIn."
assistant: "This sounds like a feature specification that would benefit from flow analysis. Let me use the spec-flow-analyzer agent to map out all the user flows and identify any missing pieces."
<commentary>
The user is describing a new feature. Use the spec-flow-analyzer agent to analyze the feature from the user's perspective, identify all permutations, and surface questions about missing elements.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: The user has created a plan for a new onboarding flow.
user: "Can you review this onboarding plan and make sure we haven't missed anything?"
assistant: "I'll use the spec-flow-analyzer agent to thoroughly analyze this onboarding plan from the user's perspective."
<commentary>
The user is explicitly asking for review of a plan. Use the spec-flow-analyzer agent to identify all user flows, edge cases, and gaps in the specification.
</commentary>
</example>

Call this agent when:
- A user presents a feature specification, plan, or requirements document
- A user asks to review or validate a design or implementation plan
- A user describes a new feature or integration that needs flow analysis
- After initial planning sessions to validate completeness
- Before implementation begins on complex user-facing features
- When stakeholders need clarity on user journeys and edge cases (Tools: All tools)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- posthog:error-analyzer: Analyze multiple PostHog errors in parallel to identify patterns, root causes, and prioritize fixes based on user impact. (Tools: All tools)
- reviewer: Code review agent - critically reviews changes for quality, security, and correctness (Tools: All tools)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- test-doc: Use this agent when the user needs markdown files created in the test-files/ directory. This includes generating test data files, sample documentation, mock content, or any markdown-formatted files for testing purposes.

Examples:

<example>
Context: User needs sample markdown files for testing a documentation parser.
user: "I need some sample markdown files to test my parser"
assistant: "I'll use the markdown-file-generator agent to create sample markdown files in the test-files/ directory for your parser testing."
<Task tool invocation to launch markdown-file-generator agent>
</example>

Context: User is setting up test fixtures and needs markdown content.
user: "Create a few test markdown files with different heading levels and formatting"
assistant: "Let me use the markdown-file-generator agent to create markdown files with varied formatting in the test-files/ directory."
<Task tool invocation to launch markdown-file-generator agent>
</example>

Context: User needs mock README files for testing.
user: "Generate some fake README files for my test suite"
assistant: "I'll invoke the markdown-file-generator agent to create mock README files in the test-files/ directory."
<Task tool invocation to launch markdown-file-generator agent>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- diagnose: Disciplined diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Reproduce → minimise → hypothesise → instrument → fix → regression-test. Use when user says "diagnose this" / "debug this", reports a bug, says something is broken/throwing/failing, or describes a performance regression.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- github-triage: Triage GitHub issues through a label-based state machine. Use when user wants to create an issue, triage issues, review incoming bugs or feature requests, prepare issues for an AFK agent, or manage issue workflow.
- grill-me: Interview the user relentlessly about a plan or design until reaching shared understanding, resolving each branch of the decision tree. Use when user wants to stress-test a plan, get grilled on their design, or mentions "grill me".
- humanizer: Remove signs of AI-generated writing from text. Use when editing or reviewing
text to make it sound more natural and human-written. Based on Wikipedia's
comprehensive "Signs of AI writing" guide. Detects and fixes patterns including:
inflated symbolism, promotional language, superficial -ing analyses, vague
attributions, em dash overuse, rule of three, AI vocabulary words, negative
parallelisms, and excessive conjunctive phrases.
- review-pr-feedback: Walk every unresolved review thread on the current branch's PR — fix what is fixable, ask the user about anything ambiguous, then reply on each thread and mark it resolved. Use when the user says "review PR feedback", "go thru the PR comments", "address review comments", or similar.
- ship: Commit, push, and update the PR description or add a comment based on new changes. Use when the user says "ship it", "commit push and update pr", or similar.
- tdd: Test-driven development with red-green-refactor loop. Use when user wants to build features or fix bugs using TDD, mentions "red-green-refactor", wants integration tests, or asks for test-first development.
- to-issues: Break a plan, spec, or PRD into independently-grabbable GitHub issues using tracer-bullet vertical slices. Use when user wants to convert a plan into issues, create implementation tickets, or break down work into issues.
- to-prd: Turn the current conversation context into a PRD and submit it as a GitHub issue. Use when user wants to create a PRD from the current context.
- write-a-skill: Create new agent skills with proper structure, progressive disclosure, and bundled resources. Use when user wants to create, write, or build a new skill.

For individual phases, use /agent-integration:research, /agent-integration:write-tests, or /agent-integration:implement. Use when the user says "integrate agent", "add agent support", or wants to run the full agent integration pipeline end-to-end.

For individual phases, use /e2e:triage-ci, /e2e:debug, or /e2e:implement. Use when the user says "triage e2e", "fix e2e failures", or wants the full triage-to-fix pipeline.

- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

content.text:
Fetched all three — trail #1059 (`fix/uninstall-external-agent-hooks`), all open, all against the current code version.

**1. HIGH — `cmd/entire/cli/setup.go:2436` — uninstall confirm has no TTY guard**
`runUninstall`'s `form.Run()` isn't gated on `interactive.CanPromptInteractively()`, unlike the other three prompts in the file (`:470`, `:1745`, `:2319`). huh's bubbletea opens `/dev/tty` directly, so a non-interactive `entire disable --uninstall` without `--force` fails with `confirmation cancelled: huh: bubbletea: error opening TTY: ... device not configured` instead of being told about `--force`. Violates the agent-safe CLI rule in CLAUDE.md.
→ **Has an attached patch**: adds the `CanPromptInteractively()` guard printing "Re-run with --force to uninstall non-interactively." and returning a `SilentError`. Reviewer says `go build ./cmd/...` + gofmt clean.

**2. MEDIUM — `cmd/entire/cli/setup_test.go:1301` — `TestRunUninstall_SummaryNamesExternalAgent` hangs under a pty**
Same root cause. It's the only test in `cmd/entire/cli` that drives a huh form (`force=false`), and it only passes in CI because `/dev/tty` is unavailable — stdin redirection is irrelevant since bubbletea reads `/dev/tty`. Under a pty it renders the confirm and waits forever (reviewer showed rc=142 at a 25s alarm). So `mise run test` from a developer terminal hangs, and CI can't catch it. Fixed by finding #1's patch — `testing.Testing()` makes `CanPromptInteractively()` false, and all 6 `TestRunUninstall_*` then pass in 5s.

**3. LOW — `cmd/entire/cli/setup.go:2531` — `UninstallHooks` runs on unenabled external plugins**
`wasInstalled` is computed but only used for the printout; `UninstallHooks` runs unconditionally on every registered agent. Now that `external.DiscoverAndRegister` is on this path (`setup.go:2385`), `entire disable --uninstall` invokes the mutating `uninstall-hooks` subcommand on every `entire-agent-*` binary on `$PATH`, including plugins the user never enabled. That's in tension with the stated rationale for gating discovery — the gate decides *whether* plugins run, but once on, unenabled ones get a write command. Suggested: `continue` when `!wasInstalled` for external agents, or state in the PR body that the fan-out is intended.

Findings 1 and 2 are one fix. Want me to apply the attached patch (`entire trail finding apply`) and then decide on #3?

# Ship Changes

Commit current changes, push to remote, and update the PR.

## Step 1: Analyze changes

1. Run `git diff --stat` and `git diff` to understand what changed
2. Run `git status` to see untracked files
3. Run `git log --oneline -3` to match the repo's commit message style

## Step 2: Commit

1. Stage only the relevant changed/untracked files by name (never `git add -A` or `git add .`)
2. Write a concise commit message that focuses on the "why" not the "what"
   - If `` is provided, use it as the commit message
   - Otherwise, draft one from the diff
3. Commit. If hooks fail, diagnose and fix — do NOT use `--no-verify`

## Step 3: Push

1. Check if the branch tracks a remote: `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref --symbolic-full-name @{u}`
2. If not tracking, push with `-u origin <branch>`
3. If tracking, just `git push`
4. If push is rejected (remote has new commits), pull with rebase first then push

## Step 4: Update PR

1. Find the open PR for the current branch: `gh pr view --json number,body,title`
2. If no PR exists, skip this step and inform the user
3. Compare the current PR body against the new changes:
   - If the changes are within the existing PR scope, update the description to reflect the current state
   - If the changes are additive or a follow-up, add a PR comment summarizing what was just pushed instead
4. When updating the PR body, preserve the overall structure but refresh the summary bullets and test plan
5. When adding a comment, keep it concise — bullet points of what changed and why
6. **Before making any PR update (description edit or comment), show the user the exact text you plan to post and ask for their approval. Do NOT post until they confirm.**

## Rules

- Never commit files that look like secrets (.env, credentials, tokens)
- Never force push

content.text:
The decision I made, and the parts I'd push back on myself:

**What I chose:** skip only for external agents (`!wasInstalled && external.IsExternal(ag)`), keeping built-ins unconditional.

**The argument for it:** the discovery gate's stated rationale is "uninstalling is not a reason to start executing plugins they never authorized." Once the gate is on, an unconditional `UninstallHooks` invokes a *mutating* subcommand on every `entire-agent-*` on `$PATH` — a plugin author's `uninstall-hooks` can do whatever it likes, so this is qualitatively different from a built-in's in-process no-op.

**Three things worth your call:**

1. **The asymmetry is a wart.** `!wasInstalled && external.IsExternal(ag)` reads as a special case, and it costs a comment to justify. The uniform alternative — `if !wasInstalled { continue }` for everyone — is simpler and arguably more honest: if `AreHooksInstalled` can't be trusted, the belt-and-braces call is papering over a bug in it rather than fixing it. I kept the split because the `AnyGitHookInstalled` comment 100 lines up shows the codebase deliberately does distrust its own detection for stale hooks, and widening the skip could silently strand a hook an older Entire wrote. But if you think that concern doesn't apply to agent hooks, the uniform version is the better code.

2. **`are-hooks-installed` now runs twice per external plugin** — once in `GetAgentsWithHooksInstalled` for the summary, once here. Visible in the test's exec log (`info / are-hooks-installed / are-hooks-installed`). Two subprocess spawns per plugin on `$PATH`. Pre-existing, not something my change introduced, and out of scope — but it's the kind of thing that gets worse as plugin count grows.

3. **The finding offered "or state in the PR body that it's intended"** and I didn't take that option. Defensible either way: fanning out to every discovered plugin *could* be argued as desirable (a plugin whose `are-hooks-installed` is buggy still gets cleaned). I judged the authorization argument stronger, but that's a product call about plugin trust, not a correctness one — so if you disagree, reverting to the documented-behavior option is a one-line revert plus a PR-body note, and the test I added would come out with it.

Which way do you want it?

{"body":"<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/1059
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Summary
`entire disable --uninstall` reports success while leaving an external agent's hooks installed.

Reproduced on a repo with `external_agents: true` and an external plugin whose `are-hooks-installed` reports true:

```
$ entire disable --uninstall --force

Uninstalling Entire CLI...
  Removed Claude Code hooks
  Removed git hooks (5)
  Removed .entire directory

Entire CLI uninstalled successfully.

$ # subcommands the plugin was asked to run: (empty — it was never executed, not even `info`)
```

The plugin's hooks stay on disk, and because `.entire/` (settings included) has just been deleted, what remains is a set of agent hooks calling into an Entire that is no longer installed there.

## Cause
`runUninstall` and `removeAgentHooks` reach agents only through the registry — `GetAgentsWithHooksInstalled` and `agent.List()` — and nothing on that path ever runs external-agent discovery, so an external agent is not in the registry to be uninstalled. Uninstalling an external agent's hooks necessarily means calling back into its plugin, which is exactly what the other commands that must call into a plugin (`review`, `resume`, `attach`, the hooks trees) already run discovery for.

## Fix
One `external.DiscoverAndRegister(ctx)` at the top of `runUninstall`. `removeAgentHooks` has exactly one caller (`runUninstall`), reached only from `entire disable --uninstall` (`setup.go:1100`) — `entire clean` does not touch agent hooks — so that single call covers the path.

**Gated, not `…Always`.** Enabling an external agent (`entire agent add <plugin>` or `entire enable --agent <plugin>`) persists `external_agents=true`, so a repo with an installed external agent already has the gate on. The gate is the user's authorization for the CLI to execute their plugins, and uninstalling is not a reason to start executing plugins they never authorized.

## Scope — what this does NOT fix
The `"Entire is not installed in this repository"` early return is **not** covered, deliberately and unavoidably with this approach: that branch is only reachable when `!entireDirExists`, and once `.entire/` is gone the `external_agents` setting is unreadable, so gated discovery no-ops. Whenever `.entire/` exists, `entireDirExists` already prevents the early return. So a repo whose `.entire/` was removed by hand while external agent hooks remain still reports "not installed" and leaves them.

## Test
Both written red first — the exec-log file did not exist at all, and the summary printed only `.entire/ directory`:

- `TestRunUninstall_RemovesExternalAgentHooks`: the mock plugin's exec log contains `uninstall-hooks`, i.e. the plugin was actually called.
- `TestRunUninstall_SummaryNamesExternalAgent`: the confirmation summary names the external agent instead of silently omitting it.

## Verification
- `mise run fmt` — clean
- `mise run lint` (golangci-lint 2.11.3) — 0 issues
- `go test ./cmd/entire/cli/ ./cmd/entire/cli/agent/... -count=1` — all pass

## Note on the base
Opened against `fix/1928-agent-group-external-discovery` because that is the branch it is currently pushed on top of. The patch is in fact self-contained — `git range-diff` shows it identical when rebased straight onto `main` — so it can be retargeted at `main` instead if that is preferred, rather than waiting on #1930.

---
Pushed `925d77740`, addressing the three review findings on trail 1059.

**TTY guard on the uninstall confirm** (`setup.go`, high + medium findings — one root cause)

Applied the suggested patch as-is: `runUninstall`'s confirm now returns early via `CanPromptInteractively()` instead of dropping into huh, so a non-interactive caller is pointed at `--force` rather than getting `huh: bubbletea: error opening TTY`.

This also fixes a test that was passing for the wrong reason. `TestRunUninstall_SummaryNamesExternalAgent` (added in this PR) drives a huh form with `force=false`, and only terminated because CI has no `/dev/tty` — bubbletea reads `/dev/tty`, not stdin, so `go test`'s stdin is irrelevant. Under a pty it rendered the prompt and hung indefinitely, meaning `mise run test` from a developer terminal blocked there and CI could not catch it. Verified under a pty after the fix:

```
--- PASS: TestRunUninstall_SummaryNamesExternalAgent (0.26s)
    setup_test.go:1311: uninstall did not complete (expected without a terminal): uninstall confirmation requires a terminal
ok  github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli  1.241s
```

All 6 `TestRunUninstall_*` in 1.2s, versus hanging to a 25s alarm before.

**`UninstallHooks` no longer runs on unenabled plugins** (`setup.go`, low finding)

`removeAgentHooks` computed `wasInstalled` but only used it for the printout — the call itself was unconditional. Harmless while the registry held only built-ins, but the `external.DiscoverAndRegister` this PR adds registers every `entire-agent-*` on `$PATH`, not just the one `entire agent add` chose, so uninstall invoked the plugin's mutating `uninstall-hooks` against plugins the user never enabled. That reaches past the discovery gate whose rationale is stated in the Fix section above.

External agents reporting no hooks installed are now skipped. Built-ins keep the unconditional call: it is in-process and idempotent, and still clears hooks a stale `AreHooksInstalled` fails to recognize — the same reasoning as `AnyGitHookInstalled` a few lines up.

`TestRunUninstall_SkipsUnenabledExternalAgent` pins it, written red first — the exec log showed `info / are-hooks-installed / are-hooks-installed / uninstall-hooks`.

**Verification** — `mise run fmt` clean; golangci-lint `--new-from-rev=HEAD` 0 issues; `mise run test:ci` fully green including both canaries (56 vogon + 4 roger-roger E2E).

One thing I did not do: `are-hooks-installed` now runs twice per external plugin per uninstall (once for the confirmation summary, once in `removeAgentHooks`) — two subprocess spawns per plugin on `$PATH`. Pre-existing and out of scope here, noting it as it scales with plugin count.

---

<cross-session-message from="uds:/tmp/cc-socks/40815.sock" from-name="uninstall-ext-a9" from-mode="prompting">
Review of `fix/uninstall-external-agent-hooks` (trail 1110) came back with 5 points. #3 was a question, answered below, no code change. Please implement 1, 2, 4, 5. All in `cmd/entire/cli/setup.go`, `cmd/entire/cli/config.go`, `cmd/entire/cli/agent/`, `cmd/entire/cli/agent/external/`, plus tests.

Context: I verified `go test ./cmd/entire/cli/` passes (also `-shuffle=on`), `golangci-lint --new-from-rev=main` is clean, and the core fix is correct. These are follow-ups, not a rewrite.

---

## 1. Do not change the current contract for built-in agents

`setup.go:2506` gates the new "uninstalled, but some agent hooks could not be removed" message + `SilentError` (non-zero exit) on `agentHooksErr != nil`. But `errs` in `removeAgentHooks` collects failures from **built-in** agents too, so a built-in `UninstallHooks` failure now flips exit status where it used to be a warning + `uninstalled successfully` + exit 0.

The justification written into that comment — unreachable from a re-run once `.entire/` is gone — is only true for external agents. A built-in is perfectly reachable on a re-run: leftover hooks keep the installed set non-empty, so the `Entire is not installed in this repository.` early return does not fire.

Gate the new message and the non-zero exit on `len(failedExternal) > 0`, not on `agentHooksErr != nil`. Built-in failures keep exactly the old behaviour: `Warning: failed to remove agent hooks: ...` on stderr, `uninstalled successfully` on stdout, exit 0. Update the comment so it stops claiming the re-run argument for built-ins.

## 2. Track probe failure separately from "no hooks installed", and say so

`external.Agent.AreHooksInstalled` (`agent/external/external.go`) collapses subprocess failure, timeout, and malformed JSON into `false`. So an external plugin that *does* have hooks but cannot answer is skipped by the `!wasInstalled[name] && external.IsExternal(ag)` guard, and the run still prints `uninstalled successfully`. Today the only trace is a `logging.Debug`, which the user never sees — and this run is their last chance, which is the whole argument the failure path already makes.

Plumb the error through so a failed probe is distinguishable, then act on it:

- **agent package**: add an optional, error-aware probe capability alongside `HookSupport`, e.g.
  ```go
  // HookInstallProbe reports hooks-installed state with a failed probe
  // distinguished from a clean "no". HookSupport.AreHooksInstalled collapses
  // both into false, which is fine for display but not for deciding whether to
  // skip a plugin during uninstall.
  type HookInstallProbe interface {
      ProbeHooksInstalled(ctx context.Context) (bool, error)
  }
  ```
  with an `AsHookInstallProbe(ag Agent) (HookInstallProbe, bool)` accessor. Plain type assertion — no `DeclaredCaps` gate; it is a refinement of an already-declared `Hooks` capability, so follow the `AsHookFreshness` doc-comment style and explain why no declaration is needed. Built-in agents simply do not implement it and keep going through `AreHooksInstalled`.

- **external package**: implement `ProbeHooksInstalled` on `*Agent` as the error-returning form of the existing method, and refactor `AreHooksInstalled` to call it and swallow the error, so there is one code path. Forward it from `wrappedAgent` / `wrappedAgentWithProtectedFiles` next to the existing `AreHooksInstalled` forwarders in `capabilities.go`.

- **config.go**: one sweep must yield both answers, since detect-once is the property this branch already committed to. Add
  ```go
  // AgentHookState is the result of one hooks-installed sweep.
  type AgentHookState struct {
      Installed   []types.AgentName // reported hooks installed
      ProbeFailed []types.AgentName // could not answer; installed state unknown
  }
  func GetAgentHookState(ctx context.Context) AgentHookState
  ```
  and reduce `GetAgentsWithHooksInstalled` to `return GetAgentHookState(ctx).Installed` so its seven existing callers are untouched. Populate `ProbeFailed` only from `AsHookInstallProbe` agents whose probe errored.

4. agent/agent/testing.go with SnapshotRegistryForTesting (registryMu for clone and restore, maps.Clone).

5. Both: single `if len(failedExternal) > 0` wrapping loop + trailing line; agentDisplayName extracted and agentDisplayNames rewritten to call it; prose uses the display name, the command keeps the registry name.

TWO DEVIATIONS

A. Item 4 is a PREREQUISITE for item 2, not hygiene. With the snapshot only in installExternalAgentPluginForUninstall as you specified, TestRunUninstall_SkipsUnenabledExternalAgent failed immediately and TestRunUninstall_Force_RemovesEntireDirectory failed under -shuffle=on, both with "some agent hooks could not be removed". Mechanism: a leaked plugin's binary is gone with its TempDir, so its probe now ERRORS instead of returning false, so item 2 stops skipping it, attempts uninstall-hooks, and that fails. Item 2 converts every pre-existing leak into a cross-test failure.

So I put t.Cleanup(SnapshotRegistryForTesting()) in writeExternalAgentBinaryEx and writeExternalSummaryAgentBinary instead — every leak path goes through a mock-binary writer, and there are ~8 call sites across setup_test.go and explain_summary_provider_test.go, not just the uninstall helper. Nested calls are fine: LIFO restore ends at the pre-test snapshot. I dropped the leak paragraph from the uninstall helper's doc comment as you asked and put the rationale on the writer.

B. AsHookInstallProbe uses the existing builtinCapability helper, whose doc said "built-in-only capabilities". This capability is external-only, so the name now reads wrong at that one call site. I widened the helper's doc ("built-in-only ones, and ones that refine a capability already declared") rather than renaming it to ungatedCapability across its 8 call sites, to keep the diff off files you may be editing. If you'd rather have the rename, it's mechanical — say so and I'll do it.

ONE THING TO CHECK, NOT A DISAGREEMENT

The fake built-in agent embeds *vogon.Agent (concrete, not the agent.Agent interface — embedding the interface silently fails AsHookSupport, since HookNames/ParseHookEvent/InstallHooks don't promote). That gives the fake vogon's IsTestOnly() == true. It doesn't affect these tests (nothing in runUninstall filters on TestOnly), but if you later assert over StringList() it would be invisible there.

cd /Users/gtrrz-victor/wks/cli/uninstall-ext; git commit -F - <<'MSG' 2>&1 | tail -6
Keep the non-zero uninstall exit for external agents only

The failure path added for leftover agent hooks gated on any UninstallHooks
error, so a built-in failure also flipped the exit status where it used to be a
warning and a zero exit. The argument for that treatment does not hold for
built-ins: the hooks are unreachable from a re-run only because .entire/ — and
with it the setting gating external discovery — has just been deleted. A
built-in is always reachable, since its leftover hooks keep the installed set
non-empty and the "not installed here" early return never fires.

Gate the message and the SilentError on the failed-external list instead.

Also pin the built-in/external asymmetry, which nothing covered: a built-in
absent from the installed set is still asked to uninstall, because the call is
in-process, idempotent, and catches hook config that is stale in a way
AreHooksInstalled does not recognise. Only external plugins — where the call is
a mutating subprocess against a binary discovery found on $PATH rather than one
the user enabled — are skipped on a clean "no hooks".

Testing a built-in means registering a fake, which the process-global agent
registry has no way to undo, so add a snapshot/restore seam and use it wherever
these tests write a mock plugin: a leaked entry outlives the TempDir holding its
binary, and later tests walking List() then exec a path that is gone.

<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/1110
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Summary
`entire disable --uninstall` reports success while leaving an external agent's hooks installed.

Reproduced on a repo with `external_agents: true` and an external plugin whose `are-hooks-installed` reports true:

```
$ entire disable --uninstall --force

Uninstalling Entire CLI...
  Removed Claude Code hooks
  Removed git hooks (5)
  Removed .entire directory

Entire CLI uninstalled successfully.

$ # subcommands the plugin was asked to run: (empty — it was never executed, not even `info`)
```

The plugin's hooks stay on disk, and because `.entire/` (settings included) has just been deleted, what remains is a set of agent hooks calling into an Entire that is no longer installed there.

## Cause
`runUninstall` and `removeAgentHooks` reach agents only through the registry — `GetAgentsWithHooksInstalled` and `agent.List()` — and nothing on that path ever runs external-agent discovery, so an external agent is not in the registry to be uninstalled. Uninstalling an external agent's hooks necessarily means calling back into its plugin, which is exactly what the other commands that must call into a plugin (`review`, `resume`, `attach`, the hooks trees) already run discovery for.

## Fix
One `external.DiscoverAndRegister(ctx)` at the top of `runUninstall`. `removeAgentHooks` has exactly one caller (`runUninstall`), reached only from `entire disable --uninstall` (`setup.go:1100`) — `entire clean` does not touch agent hooks — so that single call covers the path.

**Gated, not `…Always`.** Enabling an external agent (`entire agent add <plugin>` or `entire enable --agent <plugin>`) persists `external_agents=true`, so a repo with an installed external agent already has the gate on. The gate is the user's authorization for the CLI to execute their plugins, and uninstalling is not a reason to start executing plugins they never authorized.

## Follow-ups from review
Discovery on this path changed what `removeAgentHooks` is doing, so four things had to follow it:

- **The confirm prompt now has a TTY guard** (`925d7774`). It ran `huh` with no `interactive.CanPromptInteractively()` check, unlike the other three prompts in this file. huh's bubbletea opens `/dev/tty` directly, so a non-interactive caller got `huh: bubbletea: error opening TTY` instead of being told about `--force`. This also meant `TestRunUninstall_SummaryNamesExternalAgent` passed only because CI has no `/dev/tty`; under a pty it rendered the prompt and hung indefinitely, so `mise run test` from a developer terminal blocked there and CI could not catch it.
- **Hooks-installed is detected once per uninstall, not twice** (`f363633`). The confirmation summary and the removal each ran their own sweep; for an external agent that is a subprocess per plugin on `$PATH`. The removal now reuses the sweep the summary was built from, so it uninstalls exactly what the user was shown.
- **A plugin whose `uninstall-hooks` fails is named, with the command that still works** (`6a16fb97`, narrowed in `682b6d35`). A bare warning is unactionable for an external agent: step 4 deletes `.entire/`, and with it the setting gating discovery, so a re-run cannot even see the plugin to retry it. This run is the user's only chance to learn its hooks were left behind.
- **`UninstallHooks` is no longer run against plugins the user never enabled** (`925d7774`). It was called unconditionally, which was harmless while the registry held only built-ins — but discovery registers every `entire-agent-*` on `$PATH`, not just the one `entire agent add` chose, so uninstall invoked the plugin's *mutating* `uninstall-hooks` against all of them. That reaches past the gate whose rationale is stated above. External agents reporting no hooks installed are now skipped.

Built-ins deliberately keep the unconditional call: it is in-process, idempotent, and still clears hook config that is stale in a way `AreHooksInstalled` does not recognise as installed — the same reasoning as `AnyGitHookInstalled` a few lines above. That asymmetry is now pinned by a test.

## Behaviour change
`entire disable --uninstall` **exits non-zero** when an *external* plugin's `uninstall-hooks` fails, printing `Entire CLI uninstalled, but some agent hooks could not be removed` rather than `uninstalled successfully`. A script wrapping the command sees the partial uninstall instead of a false success.

A **built-in** failure is unchanged: warning on stderr, `uninstalled successfully`, exit 0. The non-zero exit is reserved for the unreachable-on-re-run case, and a built-in is always reachable — its leftover hooks keep the installed set non-empty, so the `Entire is not installed in this repository.` early return never fires.

## Scope — what this does NOT fix
The `"Entire is not installed in this repository"` early return is **not** covered, deliberately and unavoidably with this approach: that branch is only reachable when `!entireDirExists`, and once `.entire/` is gone the `external_agents` setting is unreadable, so gated discovery no-ops. Whenever `.entire/` exists, `entireDirExists` already prevents the early return. So a repo whose `.entire/` was removed by hand while external agent hooks remain still reports "not installed" and leaves them.

Distinguishing the two means widening the agent interface, which does not belong in this PR; it needs its own.

Written red first — the exec-log file did not exist at all, and the summary printed only `.entire/ directory`:

content.text:
Two open findings, both `current`, both on code from this branch.

**1. MEDIUM — `setup.go:2586` — the skip silently swallows a crashed probe** (no patch)

This is the hole I flagged yesterday, now with a reproduction. A mock whose `are-hooks-installed` exits 3 with hooks genuinely on disk:

```
Entire CLI uninstalled successfully.
STDERR: (empty)
err = <nil>
>>> uninstall-hooks was NEVER called
```

Hooks left behind, success reported, exit 0. The reviewer's sharpest point is one I'd missed: **this is a regression, not just an unclosed gap.** Before `925d7774` the unconditional `UninstallHooks` did remove those hooks. My skip introduced it.

It also demolishes the justification I wrote into that comment — that there's nothing user-facing to say because the summary already showed no hooks. With `--force` there's no summary at all, and interactively the summary is repeating a claim derived from a probe that crashed. That comment is wrong as written.

The reviewer independently concludes the fix needs an error-returning probe on the external agent, spanning `external.go` — which is exactly the interface change you ruled out of scope. So the finding and your scope call are in direct tension, and it's your call to resolve:

- **Fix it here** — reinstates the interface work you rejected.
- **Revert just the skip** for probe-failures — impossible without knowing a probe failed, which is the same interface change.
- **Accept the regression and document it** — the Scope section already describes the hole; I'd add that it's a regression against pre-`925d7774` behavior, and file a follow-up.

Also worth noting: `mise run test:ci` passed throughout, because every mock's `are-hooks-installed` exits 0. Nothing in the suite covers a failing probe.

**2. LOW — `setup.go:2470` — the recovery command doesn't honor the plugin protocol** (patch attached, applies cleanly per the reviewer)

`docs/architecture/external-agent-protocol.md:16-23` guarantees every subcommand `ENTIRE_REPO_ROOT`, `ENTIRE_PROTOCOL_VERSION`, and a repo-root working directory, and `external.go:446-453` does supply all three. So the bare `entire-agent-<name> uninstall-hooks` I print can be rejected by a conforming plugin — and it drops the `.exe`/`.bat` suffix on Windows. Since that line exists precisely because it's the user's last chance before `.entire/` is deleted, printing a command that may not run defeats it.

The patch prints `cd <root> && ENTIRE_REPO_ROOT=… ENTIRE_PROTOCOL_VERSION=… entire-agent-<name> uninstall-hooks`. Note it addresses the env vars but **not** the Windows suffix, which the finding raises in the same breath — so applying it leaves half the finding standing.

Want me to apply #2 and hold #1 pending your scope decision?

content.text:
The name is still printed bare as `entire-agent-<name>`.

I over-conceded on that point earlier, though, and it changes what's actually left to do: **the missing `.exe` is not a real problem.** Windows resolves extensionless commands through `PATHEXT` (`.COM;.EXE;.BAT;.CMD;…`), so typing `entire-agent-foo uninstall-hooks` in cmd.exe or PowerShell finds `entire-agent-foo.exe` or `.bat` on its own — and Git Bash/MSYS does the same. The registry name is the binary's basename minus the suffix (`discovery.go:173` strips it via `StripExeExt`), so re-adding it would be cosmetic. The finding raised it, but it doesn't break the command.

What *is* genuinely broken on Windows is the shell syntax the patch introduced: `cd X && VAR=y prog` is POSIX-only. cmd.exe needs `set VAR=y`, PowerShell needs `$env:VAR="y"`. So the patch fixed the protocol contract for POSIX users and made the Windows hint worse than the bare command it replaced, which at least parsed everywhere.

That's also the kind of thing CLAUDE.md warns about for Windows command construction, though the rule there is about commands Entire *executes* — this is printed text a human copies, so nothing silently truncates. Fixing it means branching the printed form on `runtime.GOOS`, which is self-contained and needs no interface change, unlike the still-open medium finding.

Real, but weaker than stated — and it points at a worse bug it doesn't mention.

**As stated:** near-unreachable. `name` comes from `agent.List()` and `agent.Get(name)` succeeded seconds earlier inside `removeAgentHooks`; production code has no unregister path (`SnapshotRegistryForTesting` is test-only), so the registry only grows within one command. **What it misses:** the same empty string is worse in the two *list* callers. `agentDisplayNames` drops a failed lookup entirely, so a missing agent silently vanishes from `Enabled agents:` (`setup.go:459`) and from the uninstall summary's `Agent hooks (…)` (`setup.go:2421`). That's the same failure an earlier finding on this branch already objected to — a plugin silently absent from the summary the user approves. I preserved that behavior when I extracted the helper rather than questioning it.

So the fix I'd make is one line deeper than suggested: have `agentDisplayName` fall back to `string(name)`, then let `agentDisplayNames` append unconditionally. That fixes the malformed prose, stops the silent drops, and removes the `""` check. No test pins the current behavior.

content.text:
By the time we decide to skip, we've already executed that binary twice — `info` during discovery (`external.go:38`, on every `entire-agent-*` on `$PATH`), then `are-hooks-installed` in the sweep. The exec log from the tests shows it plainly:

```
info
are-hooks-installed
uninstall-hooks
```

So the framing I used for the skip — "don't start executing plugins the user never authorized" — is really the justification for *gating discovery*, and that gate is `external_agents=true`. It says nothing about the skip. Once discovery runs, every plugin on `$PATH` gets executed regardless. The only thing the skip actually buys is not sending a **mutating** subcommand to a plugin that just said it has nothing to remove — a much narrower claim than the one in my comment, and a conforming plugin's `uninstall-hooks` with no hooks installed should be a no-op anyway.

That gives you a fourth option on the open finding, and a better one than the three I listed: **drop the skip and go back to unconditional `UninstallHooks`.** It closes the regression outright, needs no interface change, and its cost is re-opening the original low finding — whose premise is weaker than it looked, since we're already running those binaries.

The honest ledger for that trade:
- **Against:** a plugin the user never enabled gets a write command. Real, but it already gets two reads, and it only gets any of them because the user turned the gate on.
- **For:** no plugin's hooks silently survive an uninstall that reports success, which is the bug this whole PR exists to fix.

If you want it, it's roughly a revert of the skip plus deleting `TestRunUninstall_SkipsUnenabledExternalAgent` — and inverting it, since a plugin reporting no hooks would then still be asked.

// runUninstall completely removes Entire from the repository.
func runUninstall(ctx context.Context, w, errW io.Writer, force bool) error {
	// Check if we're in a git repository
	repoRoot, rootErr := paths.WorktreeRoot(ctx)
	if rootErr != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(errW, "Not a git repository. Nothing to uninstall.")
		return NewSilentError(errors.New("not a git repository"))
	}

	// Uninstall reaches an agent only through the registry, and an external
	// agent's hooks can only be removed by calling back into its plugin. Without
	// discovery the plugin is invisible here: it is absent from the confirmation
	// summary, and its UninstallHooks never runs, so its hooks survive an
	// uninstall that reports success.
	//
	// Gated, not Always: enabling an external agent (`entire agent add <plugin>`
	// or `entire enable --agent <plugin>`) persists external_agents=true, so an
	// installed external agent implies the gate is on. The gate is the user's
	// authorization for the CLI to execute their plugins, and uninstalling is not
	// a reason to start executing ones they never authorized.
	external.DiscoverAndRegister(ctx)

	// Gather counts for display
	sessionStateCount := countSessionStates(ctx)
	shadowBranchCount := countShadowBranches(ctx)
	// AnyGitHookInstalled, not IsGitHookInstalled: a hook left by an older
	// version is stale but still ours, and uninstall must still offer to remove
	// it rather than reporting that Entire is not installed here.
	gitHooksInstalled := strategy.AnyGitHookInstalled(ctx)
	agentsWithInstalledHooks := GetAgentsWithHooksInstalled(ctx)
	entireDirExists := checkEntireDirExists(ctx)

	// Check if there's anything to uninstall
	if !entireDirExists && !gitHooksInstalled && sessionStateCount == 0 &&
		shadowBranchCount == 0 && len(agentsWithInstalledHooks) == 0 {
		fmt.Fprintln(w, "Entire is not installed in this repository.")
		return nil
	}

	// Show confirmation prompt unless --force
	if !force {
		fmt.Fprintln(w, "\nThis will completely remove Entire from this repository:")
		if entireDirExists {
			fmt.Fprintln(w, "  - .entire/ directory")
		}
		if gitHooksInstalled {
			fmt.Fprintln(w, "  - Git hooks (prepare-commit-msg, commit-msg, post-commit, pre-push)")
		}
		if sessionStateCount > 0 {
			fmt.Fprintf(w, "  - Session state files (%d)\n", sessionStateCount)
		}
		if shadowBranchCount > 0 {
			fmt.Fprintf(w, "  - Shadow branches (%d)\n", shadowBranchCount)
		}
		if len(agentsWithInstalledHooks) > 0 {
			fmt.Fprintf(w, "  - Agent hooks (%s)\n", strings.Join(agentDisplayNames(agentsWithInstalledHooks), ", "))
		}
		fmt.Fprintln(w)

		// Without this guard the confirm below reaches huh, whose bubbletea
		// program opens /dev/tty directly. A caller with no terminal gets a
		// bubbletea internal error instead of the flag that unblocks them, and a
		// `go test` run that happens to have a controlling terminal blocks on a
		// rendered prompt.
		if !interactive.CanPromptInteractively() {
			fmt.Fprintln(errW, "No terminal available to confirm the uninstall. Re-run with --force to uninstall non-interactively.")
			return NewSilentError(errors.New("uninstall confirmation requires a terminal"))
		}

		var confirmed bool
		form := NewAccessibleForm(
			huh.NewGroup(
				huh.NewConfirm().
					Title("Are you sure you want to uninstall Entire?").
					Affirmative("Yes, uninstall").
					Negative("Cancel").
					Value(&confirmed),
			),
		)

		if err := form.Run(); err != nil {
			return fmt.Errorf("confirmation cancelled: %w", err)
		}

		if !confirmed {
			fmt.Fprintln(w, "Uninstall cancelled.")
			return nil
		}
	}

	fmt.Fprintln(w, "\nUninstalling Entire CLI...")

	// 1. Remove agent hooks (lowest risk)
	failedExternal, agentHooksErr := removeAgentHooks(ctx, w, agentsWithInstalledHooks)
	if agentHooksErr != nil {
		fmt.Fprintf(errW, "Warning: failed to remove agent hooks: %v\n", agentHooksErr)
	}
	// Step 4 below deletes .entire/, and with it the external_agents setting that
	// gates discovery — so once this returns, a re-run cannot even see these
	// plugins, let alone retry them. Name the command that still works, while the
	// hooks are still reachable, rather than leaving the user with a warning they
	// cannot act on. A built-in needs none of this: it is always reachable on a
	// re-run, since its leftover hooks keep the installed set non-empty.
	if len(failedExternal) > 0 {
		for _, name := range failedExternal {
			// The protocol promises every subcommand ENTIRE_REPO_ROOT,
			// ENTIRE_PROTOCOL_VERSION and a repo-root working directory
			// (docs/architecture/external-agent-protocol.md), so a plugin is
			// entitled to rely on them. Printing the bare binary hands the user a
			// command that a conforming plugin can reject.
			fmt.Fprintf(errW, "  %s hooks are still installed. Remove them with:\n", agentDisplayName(name))

	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintf(errW, "Warning: failed to remove shadow branches: %v\n", err)
	} else if branchesRemoved > 0 {

	// that the user must act on, and they are unreachable from a re-run now that

	if len(failedExternal) > 0 {

	return nil

**`removeAgentHooks`** — setup.go:2560-2613 (doc comment starts 2560, `func` at 2571):

```go
// removeAgentHooks removes hooks from all agents that support hooks. installed
// is the set the caller already detected, reused rather than re-detected: for an
// external agent AreHooksInstalled is a subprocess, and it is also what the
// confirmation summary was built from, so reusing it uninstalls exactly what the
// user was shown.
//
// The names of any external agents whose removal failed are returned alongside
// the error: the caller is about to delete the settings that make those plugins
// discoverable at all, so it needs to name them while they can still be acted
// on. Errors carry the agent's display name for the same reason.
func removeAgentHooks(ctx context.Context, w io.Writer, installed []types.AgentName) ([]types.AgentName, error) {
	wasInstalled := make(map[types.AgentName]bool, len(installed))
	for _, name := range installed {
		wasInstalled[name] = true
	}

	var errs []error
	var failedExternal []types.AgentName
	for _, name := range agent.List() {
		ag, err := agent.Get(name)
		if err != nil {
			continue
		}
		hs, ok := agent.AsHookSupport(ag)
		if !ok {
			continue
		}
		// Built-in agents get the call unconditionally: it is an in-process,
		// idempotent cleanup, and it still removes hooks a stale AreHooksInstalled
		// fails to recognize. For an external agent it is a subprocess running the
		// plugin's mutating uninstall-hooks, and discovery registered every
		// entire-agent-* binary on $PATH, not just the one the user enabled — so a
		// plugin reporting no hooks is left alone.
		if !wasInstalled[name] && external.IsExternal(ag) {
			// AreHooksInstalled collapses a crashed, timed-out, or malformed probe
			// into "not installed", so this skip can also mean "the plugin could not
			// tell us". Nothing user-facing to say — the summary already showed the
			// plugin as having no hooks — but leave a trace for `doctor bundle`.
			logging.Debug(ctx, "skipping external agent hook removal: plugin reports no hooks installed",
				"agent", string(name))
			continue
		}
		if err := hs.UninstallHooks(ctx); err != nil {
			errs = append(errs, fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", ag.Type(), err))
			if external.IsExternal(ag) {
				failedExternal = append(failedExternal, name)
			}
		} else if wasInstalled[name] {
			fmt.Fprintf(w, "  Removed %s hooks\n", ag.Type())
		}
	}
	return failedExternal, errors.Join(errs...)
}
```

Note: `errs` uses `ag.Type()` (the display-ish type), while `failedExternal` carries the registry `name` — the doc comment's "Errors carry the agent's display name" refers to `ag.Type()`.

func runUninstall(ctx context.Context, w, errW io.Writer, force bool) error {

	// summary, and its UninstallHooks never runs, so its hooks survive an

	// authorization for the CLI to execute their plugins, and uninstalling is not
	// a reason to start executing ones they never authorized.
	external.DiscoverAndRegister(ctx)

```go
// removeAgentHooks removes hooks from all agents that support hooks. installed
// is the set the caller already detected, reused rather than re-detected: for an
// external agent AreHooksInstalled is a subprocess, and it is also what the
// confirmation summary was built from, so reusing it uninstalls exactly what the
// user was shown.
//
// The names of any external agents whose removal failed are returned alongside
// the error: the caller is about to delete the settings that make those plugins
// discoverable at all, so it needs to name them while they can still be acted
// on. Errors carry the agent's display name for the same reason.
func removeAgentHooks(ctx context.Context, w io.Writer, installed []types.AgentName) ([]types.AgentName, error) {
	wasInstalled := make(map[types.AgentName]bool, len(installed))
	for _, name := range installed {
		wasInstalled[name] = true
	}

	var errs []error
	var failedExternal []types.AgentName
	for _, name := range agent.List() {
		ag, err := agent.Get(name)
		if err != nil {
			continue
		}
		hs, ok := agent.AsHookSupport(ag)
		if !ok {
			continue
		}
		// Built-in agents get the call unconditionally: it is an in-process,
		// idempotent cleanup, and it still removes hooks a stale AreHooksInstalled
		// fails to recognize. For an external agent it is a subprocess running the
		// plugin's mutating uninstall-hooks, and discovery registered every
		// entire-agent-* binary on $PATH, not just the one the user enabled — so a
		// plugin reporting no hooks is left alone.
		if !wasInstalled[name] && external.IsExternal(ag) {
			// AreHooksInstalled collapses a crashed, timed-out, or malformed probe
			// into "not installed", so this skip can also mean "the plugin could not
			// tell us". Nothing user-facing to say — the summary already showed the
			// plugin as having no hooks — but leave a trace for `doctor bundle`.
			logging.Debug(ctx, "skipping external agent hook removal: plugin reports no hooks installed",
				"agent", string(name))
			continue
		}
		if err := hs.UninstallHooks(ctx); err != nil {
			errs = append(errs, fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", ag.Type(), err))
			if external.IsExternal(ag) {
				failedExternal = append(failedExternal, name)
			}
		} else if wasInstalled[name] {
			fmt.Fprintf(w, "  Removed %s hooks\n", ag.Type())
		}
	}
	return failedExternal, errors.Join(errs...)
}
```

Note: `errs` uses `ag.Type()` (the display-ish type), while `failedExternal` carries the registry `name` — the doc comment's "Errors carry the agent's display name" refers to `ag.Type()`.

questions.question: Which agents get a per-plugin outcome line?

options.label: External plugins only (Recommended)
options.description: Only agents backed by an entire-agent-* binary get outcome lines. Built-ins keep today's single "Removed X hooks" line. Rationale: only externals have a subprocess that can fail or be unreachable, which is what the outcome is for.

  Removed git hooks (5)

options.label: Every hook-supporting agent
options.description: Built-ins are listed in the same outcome block as plugins, so the user sees one uniform table of what happened to each agent.

questions.question: Should a plugin that cleanly reports "no hooks installed" print a line?

options.label: Yes, list it (Recommended)
options.description: Every discovered plugin appears with its outcome, including "nothing to remove". Makes the skip visible, so a plugin that was silently passed over is no longer invisible — which is the whole complaint behind the open finding.
options.preview: other-plugin — no hooks installed, nothing to remove

options.label: No, stay silent
options.description: Only plugins we actually acted on or failed on print. Keeps the output short on machines with several plugins on $PATH, but a skipped plugin stays invisible.

questions.question: Does a probe failure alone affect the exit code?

options.label: No — only a failed removal (Recommended)
options.description: If the probe fails but the follow-up uninstall-hooks succeeds, the hooks are gone, so the uninstall succeeded: exit 0. Non-zero stays reserved for an external plugin whose uninstall-hooks actually failed, as today.

options.label: Yes — any unknown means non-zero
options.description: A plugin we could not probe makes the whole uninstall exit non-zero even if the removal then worked, on the grounds that we cannot prove the state was clean.

questions.question: If a plugin fails BOTH the probe and the uninstall, what do we tell the user?

options.label: Recovery command, as today (Recommended)
options.description: Treat it exactly like any failed uninstall: name the plugin, print the cd + env + uninstall-hooks recovery command, and exit non-zero. The probe failure is extra detail on the same line, not a separate path.

options.label: Say the binary looks broken
options.description: A plugin failing both calls is probably not runnable at all, so point at that instead of handing over a command that will likely also fail.

// runUninstall completely removes Entire from the repository.
func runUninstall(ctx context.Context, w, errW io.Writer, force bool) error {
	// Check if we're in a git repository
	repoRoot, rootErr := paths.WorktreeRoot(ctx)
	if rootErr != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(errW, "Not a git repository. Nothing to uninstall.")
		return NewSilentError(errors.New("not a git repository"))
	}

	// Uninstall reaches an agent only through the registry, and an external
	// agent's hooks can only be removed by calling back into its plugin. Without
	// discovery the plugin is invisible here: it is absent from the confirmation
	// summary, and its UninstallHooks never runs, so its hooks survive an
	// uninstall that reports success.
	//
	// Gated, not Always: enabling an external agent (`entire agent add <plugin>`
	// or `entire enable --agent <plugin>`) persists external_agents=true, so an
	// installed external agent implies the gate is on. The gate is the user's
	// authorization for the CLI to execute their plugins, and uninstalling is not
	// a reason to start executing ones they never authorized.
	external.DiscoverAndRegister(ctx)

	// Gather counts for display
	sessionStateCount := countSessionStates(ctx)
	shadowBranchCount := countShadowBranches(ctx)
	// AnyGitHookInstalled, not IsGitHookInstalled: a hook left by an older
	// version is stale but still ours, and uninstall must still offer to remove
	// it rather than reporting that Entire is not installed here.
	gitHooksInstalled := strategy.AnyGitHookInstalled(ctx)
	agentsWithInstalledHooks := GetAgentsWithHooksInstalled(ctx)
	entireDirExists := checkEntireDirExists(ctx)

	// Check if there's anything to uninstall
	if !entireDirExists && !gitHooksInstalled && sessionStateCount == 0 &&
		shadowBranchCount == 0 && len(agentsWithInstalledHooks) == 0 {
		fmt.Fprintln(w, "Entire is not installed in this repository.")
		return nil
	}

	// Show confirmation prompt unless --force
	if !force {
		fmt.Fprintln(w, "\nThis will completely remove Entire from this repository:")
		if entireDirExists {
			fmt.Fprintln(w, "  - .entire/ directory")
		}
		if gitHooksInstalled {
			fmt.Fprintln(w, "  - Git hooks (prepare-commit-msg, commit-msg, post-commit, pre-push)")
		}
		if sessionStateCount > 0 {
			fmt.Fprintf(w, "  - Session state files (%d)\n", sessionStateCount)
		}
		if shadowBranchCount > 0 {
			fmt.Fprintf(w, "  - Shadow branches (%d)\n", shadowBranchCount)
		}
		if len(agentsWithInstalledHooks) > 0 {
			fmt.Fprintf(w, "  - Agent hooks (%s)\n", strings.Join(agentDisplayNames(agentsWithInstalledHooks), ", "))

		// program opens /dev/tty directly. A caller with no terminal gets a
		// bubbletea internal error instead of the flag that unblocks them, and a
		// `go test` run that happens to have a controlling terminal blocks on a
		// rendered prompt.

			return NewSilentError(errors.New("uninstall confirmation requires a terminal"))
		}

		var confirmed bool
		form := NewAccessibleForm(
			huh.NewGroup(
				huh.NewConfirm().
					Title("Are you sure you want to uninstall Entire?").
					Affirmative("Yes, uninstall").
					Negative("Cancel").
					Value(&confirmed),
			),
		)

		if err := form.Run(); err != nil {
			return fmt.Errorf("confirmation cancelled: %w", err)
		}

		if !confirmed {
			fmt.Fprintln(w, "Uninstall cancelled.")
			return nil

	// re-run, since its leftover hooks keep the installed set non-empty.

			// command that a conforming plugin can reject.
			fmt.Fprintf(errW, "  %s hooks are still installed. Remove them with:\n", agentDisplayName(name))

// removeAgentHooks removes hooks from all agents that support hooks. installed
// is the set the caller already detected, reused rather than re-detected: for an
// external agent AreHooksInstalled is a subprocess, and it is also what the
// confirmation summary was built from, so reusing it uninstalls exactly what the
// user was shown.
//
// The names of any external agents whose removal failed are returned alongside
// the error: the caller is about to delete the settings that make those plugins
// discoverable at all, so it needs to name them while they can still be acted
// on. Errors carry the agent's display name for the same reason.
func removeAgentHooks(ctx context.Context, w io.Writer, installed []types.AgentName) ([]types.AgentName, error) {
	wasInstalled := make(map[types.AgentName]bool, len(installed))
	for _, name := range installed {
		wasInstalled[name] = true
	}

	var errs []error
	var failedExternal []types.AgentName
	for _, name := range agent.List() {
		ag, err := agent.Get(name)
		if err != nil {
			continue
		}
		hs, ok := agent.AsHookSupport(ag)
